You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the test asserts:
  - testMath320A constructs a 3x3 rank-deficient matrix and computes its SVD.
  - It expects exactly two positive singular values (the third should be zero and thus omitted) and that U·S·VT recomposes the original matrix.

- What the bug report shows:
  - For the same matrix, getSingularValues() returns three values: [11.2185997575, 0.3781791649, NaN].
  - The last should be approximately 0 (matrix is rank 2), not NaN.

- How SingularValueDecompositionImpl computes singular values:
  - The constructor reduces the input to bidiagonal form, then forms a symmetric tridiagonal matrix representing Bt·B (or B·Bt).
  - It computes the eigenvalues of this symmetric tridiagonal matrix via EigenDecompositionImpl.
  - Then:
    - It sets p to the number of eigenvalues limited by max (here max = min(m,n) = 3).
    - It trims non-positive eigenvalues only at the tail with:
      while ((p > 0) && (eigenValues[p - 1] <= 0)) { --p; }
    - It then sets singularValues[i] = sqrt(eigenValues[i]) for i in [0, p).

- Why NaN appears:
  - The trimming loop assumes non-positive eigenvalues are clustered at the end of the eigenvalues array (i.e., that eigenvalues are sorted with smallest last).
  - However, EigenDecompositionImpl does not guarantee the ordering that the SVD code relies on; due to numerical round-off, the eigenvalue that should be zero can become a small negative and appear at an arbitrary index, not necessarily at the end.
  - If a negative eigenvalue remains within the first p entries, taking sqrt on it produces NaN.
  - This explains the observed array [11.218..., 0.378..., NaN]: p stayed 3 because eigenValues[2] was positive; one of the eigenvalues in 0..2 (the last in this run) was slightly negative; sqrt of that produced NaN.

- Why the test fails:
  - The test expects two singular values. Because the trimming only removes trailing non-positives, a negative eigenvalue in any other position is not removed, resulting in 3 singular values with a NaN.
  - The first assertion (expected length 2) fails, and even if it didn’t, the value checks would fail due to NaN.

- Additional impact:
  - getS constructs a diagonal matrix directly from singularValues; a NaN there propagates into U·S·VT, potentially causing NaNs in recomposition too.
  - getU divides intermediate terms by singularValues[j]; if zeros were retained instead of excluded, it could also cause divisions by zero.

- Root cause:
  - SingularValueDecompositionImpl incorrectly assumes an order of eigenvalues when filtering out non-positive ones. It only removes trailing non-positives, leading to sqrt of negative values when a small negative eigenvalue (due to numerical error) appears elsewhere in the array.
  - The implementation should not rely on eigenvalue ordering; it should filter or clamp all non-positive eigenvalues before taking square roots (and optionally sort the remaining ones).

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
